abstract: Deleterious mutations impose genetic load, and purging them through hard selection can carry substantial demographic costs. Competitive and sexual selection can instead remove deleterious variation through differential reproductive success. What remains unclear is when this process is more efficient than equivalent hard selection, and how competition generates this advantage. Here, we use forward-time simulations to express the impact of competition as an effective selection coefficient (se) calibrated against hard selection. Competition with multiple rivals strongly amplified purifying selection, whereas repeated contests improved discrimination by averaging stochastic and environmental variation. Strong competition also reduced genetic load relative to hard selection. These effects can shift weakly deleterious mutations from drift-dominated behaviour towards efficient purging. By front-loading purifying selection into reproduction, competitive selection can reduce genetic load at lower demographic cost. This provides a population-genetic mechanism by which genic capture can translate genome-wide genetic quality into more effective purifying selection. This may be particularly important in bottlenecked populations, where demographic recovery can relax purifying selection and allow genomic erosion to persist.
